But Kamchatka is only the tip of the iceberg.

– In Singapore, a massive sinkhole suddenly opened in the city center.
– In the Philippines, Typhoon Kompasu forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands.
– In Kazakhstan and Russia, hurricane-force winds tore off roofs and downed power lines.
– In Belarus and Germany, torrential rains caused flooding and landslides.
– Southern Europe was burning once again — Türkiye, Greece, Italy, and Portugal battled large-scale wildfires.

data.text:
🛠️ Ramon Ang’s Voluntary Flood Control Initiative

In a time when accountability often feels elusive and public trust is eroded by inaction, Ramon Ang’s bold decision to lead Metro Manila’s flood control efforts—at no cost to the government or the people—is a rare and powerful act of civic leadership.

This is not merely a gesture of goodwill. It is a strategic intervention that addresses the root causes of urban flooding: clogged waterways, inadequate drainage, and the displacement of vulnerable communities. 

Through San Miguel Corporation’s Better Rivers PH program, over 8.52 million cubic meters of silt and waste have already been cleared from 163 kilometers of major rivers, restoring the natural flow of water and increasing stormwater capacity. 

Ang’s commitment to construct drainage systems, relocate families with dignity, and sustain dredging operations across critical river systems—from the Pasig and San Juan rivers to the Laguna Lake channels—demonstrates what is possible when private sector leadership aligns with public interest. 

This initiative is more than infrastructure—it is a call to action. It reminds us that solving systemic problems like flooding requires not just engineering, but empathy, vision, and shared responsibility. 

Ramon Ang’s example challenges other leaders—public and private—to rise above blame and bureaucracy, and to act with urgency and integrity.

Let this be a turning point. Let this be proof that voluntary leadership, when rooted in service, can move mountains—or in this case, rivers.
